title: Lanka, Return and the Meaning of Dharma
bigQuestion: Why do people keep retelling the Ramayana, and why do their tellings differ?

story.title: Ten Nights of the Ramayana
story.kicker: A town in India puts on the whole Ramayana as a play that lasts ten nights.
paragraphs: In a small town in North India, the autumn air is cool. Every evening, people carry mats and blankets to an open field. Strings of lights hang above a wooden stage.

This is the Ramlila, a play of Rama's life. Each night the town acts out a new part. On the first night, Rama is born. On another night, he leaves for the forest. The crowd grows bigger every evening.
The actors are neighbors: a shopkeeper, a teacher, some boys from the high school. Children in the front row know the lines by heart. They whisper them along with the actors.

On the tenth night comes the festival of Dussehra. A giant figure of Ravana stands at the edge of the field. When the play reaches the battle, the figure is set alight. Fireworks burst overhead, and the crowd cheers.
An old man in the crowd has watched this play every year since he was a boy. "It is the same story," he says, smiling. "And it is new every time." Then he joins in the cheering.
story.think: Why might people want to watch the same story every year?

lessons.title: Sita in Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: In Lanka, Sita stays strong and refuses Ravana.
reading: Ravana carries Sita to his island kingdom of *Lanka*. He keeps her in a garden of ashoka trees. He wants her to marry him. He offers her riches and a palace.
Sita refuses him every time. She stays loyal to Rama. The poem shows her as brave and strong, even though she is far from home and all alone. She waits for Rama to come.
Many Hindus honor Sita as a goddess and a model of courage and faithfulness. Some readers today also see her as a strong woman who says no to a powerful king.

words.d: Ravana's island kingdom in the Ramayana
staying true to someone

look.title: Sita Says No
look.text: Ravana boasts of his riches and power. Sita places a blade of grass between them and speaks to him without fear. She tells him she belongs to Rama and warns him to return her.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Sundara Kanda (Book 5)
look.prompt: What does Sita's answer show about her?

check.q: Where does Ravana keep Sita?
check.why: Sita is held in a garden of ashoka trees in Lanka.

check.q: What does Sita do when Ravana asks her to marry him?
check.why: Sita refuses Ravana every time.

check.q: How do many Hindus honor Sita?
choices: As a goddess and a model of courage
check.why: Many Hindus honor Sita as a goddess and a model of courage.

lessons.title: Hanuman's Journey
lessons.mainIdea: Hanuman leaps to Lanka, finds Sita and brings back word to Rama.
reading: Rama makes friends with Sugriva, king of the monkey people, called the *vanaras*. Sugriva's wise minister, Hanuman, becomes Rama's most devoted helper.
Sundara Kanda tells how Hanuman leaps across the ocean to Lanka. He searches the city at night. At last he finds Sita and gives her Rama's ring as a sign.
Hanuman is caught, and his tail is set on fire. He escapes and spreads the fire across Lanka. Then he leaps back to Rama with the good news. Many Hindus pray to Hanuman for strength and courage.

words.d: one of the monkey people who help Rama
the king of the vanaras and Rama's ally

look.title: A Hero in Many Homes
look.text: In many Hindu homes in Illinois, a small picture of Hanuman hangs near the door. Some families chant the Hanuman Chalisa, a 40-verse hymn in Hindi by tradition credited to Tulsidas, on Tuesdays.
look.prompt: What qualities of Hanuman might a family want to remember each day?

check.q: Who is Sugriva?
check.why: Sugriva is king of the monkey people and Rama's ally.

check.q: What does Hanuman give Sita?
check.why: Hanuman gives Sita Rama's ring as a sign.

check.q: Which kanda tells Hanuman's journey?
check.why: Sundara Kanda, Book 5, follows Hanuman.

lessons.title: The Bridge to Lanka
lessons.mainIdea: Rama's army builds a bridge across the sea, and Ravana's brother joins Rama.
reading: Rama's army reaches the ocean. How can they cross? The poem says a vanara named Nala leads the building of a great bridge of rocks and trees across the sea.
Folk tellings add a little squirrel who helps with grains of sand. It is not in Valmiki's poem, but many families love it. It shows that every helper counts.
Before the battle, Ravana's brother Vibhishana leaves Lanka. He tells Ravana to return Sita, but Ravana will not listen. Vibhishana joins Rama, who welcomes him.

words.d: Ravana's brother, who leaves Lanka and joins Rama
a story passed on by ordinary people, often by telling

look.title: Choosing a Side
look.text: Vibhishana is Ravana's own brother. He loves his family. But he believes Ravana is doing wrong by keeping Sita. He warns his brother, then leaves to join Rama.

check.q: Who leads the building of the bridge in Valmiki's poem?
check.why: The poem says the vanara Nala led the building.

check.q: Is the squirrel story part of Valmiki's poem?
choices: No, it comes from the Rig Veda
No, it is a folk telling
check.why: The squirrel is a well-loved folk addition.

check.q: Who is Vibhishana?
check.why: Vibhishana leaves Ravana and joins Rama.

lessons.title: The Battle
lessons.mainIdea: Rama defeats Ravana in a great battle and frees Sita.
reading: Yuddha Kanda, the "book of battle," tells of a long war in Lanka. Many warriors fight on both sides. Lakshmana is badly hurt, and Hanuman flies to bring healing herbs from a mountain.
At last Rama faces Ravana himself. The fight is long and hard. Rama wins. Many Hindus remember this victory as good winning over evil. The long war is over at last.
After the battle, Rama makes Vibhishana the new king of Lanka. He does not take Lanka for himself. The poem also shows respect for Ravana's funeral rites.

words.d: the sixth book of the Ramayana, telling the battle
winning a battle or contest

look.title: Hanuman and the Mountain
look.text: Lakshmana lies wounded. Hanuman must find a healing herb on a far mountain. He cannot tell which plant it is. So, the story says, he lifts the whole mountaintop and carries it back to the battlefield.
look.prompt: What does this scene show about Hanuman's loyalty?

check.q: What does Yuddha Kanda tell about?
check.why: Yuddha Kanda is the book of battle.

check.q: Who does Rama make king of Lanka?
check.why: Rama makes Vibhishana king and does not take Lanka.

check.q: What do many Hindus see in Rama's victory?
check.why: Many Hindus remember it as good winning over evil.

lessons.title: Coming Home
lessons.mainIdea: Rama returns to Ayodhya and is crowned king, and many Hindus remember this at Diwali.
reading: The fourteen years are over. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana fly home to Ayodhya in a flying chariot. Hanuman goes ahead to tell Bharata the news. The chariot is called Pushpaka.
Bharata gives back the kingdom joyfully. Rama is crowned king at last, with Sita as queen. The people of Ayodhya celebrate. There is music and feasting in every street.
Many Hindus remember this homecoming at Diwali, the festival of lights, when they light lamps to welcome Rama and Sita. Others remember Lakshmi or Krishna at Diwali.

words.d: made king or queen in a ceremony
returning home after being away

look.title: Lamps in Every Window
look.text: Picture Ayodhya on the night Rama returns. Rows of lamps glow on rooftops and doorsteps. Music plays. Bharata runs to meet his brother. Many Hindus light diyas at Diwali to remember this night.
look.prompt: How does the story connect to what families do at Diwali?

check.q: How long was Rama away?
check.why: Rama returns after fourteen years.

check.q: What does Bharata do when Rama returns?
check.why: Bharata happily returns the kingdom.

check.q: Which festival do many Hindus connect with Rama's return?
check.why: Many Hindus light Diwali lamps to remember Rama's return.

lessons.title: Rama Rajya
lessons.mainIdea: Rama Rajya, "the rule of Rama," is an ideal of fair and peaceful government.
reading: The poem says Rama ruled with fairness for many years. People were safe, fields were full and no one was treated unjustly. This is called *Rama Rajya*, "the rule of Rama."
Over time, Rama Rajya became an ideal, a picture of what good government could be. Mahatma Gandhi used the phrase for a fair India where the poorest people were cared for.
Others have used the phrase in different ways, and people still debate what it should mean. Many Hindus use it simply to mean a kind and just ruler. Its meaning is still discussed.

words.d: "the rule of Rama"; an ideal of fair and peaceful government
a picture of the best way something could be

look.title: What Makes a Good Ruler?
look.text: Imagine your class gets to design a fair leader. Would the leader listen to everyone? Help people who have less? Keep promises? Treat people equally? Many readers of the Ramayana ask the same questions.
look.prompt: Pick two qualities of a good leader. Explain why they matter.

check.q: What does Rama Rajya mean?
check.why: Rama Rajya means "the rule of Rama."

check.q: How did Gandhi use Rama Rajya?
choices: For a fair India that cares for the poorest
check.why: Gandhi used it for a just India caring for the poor.

check.q: What is an ideal?
choices: A picture of the best way something could be
check.why: An ideal is a picture of the best way things could be.

lessons.title: Hard Questions About Sita
lessons.mainIdea: Readers ask hard questions about how Sita is treated, and they answer in different ways.
reading: After the battle, Valmiki's poem says Rama doubts Sita, because she lived in Ravana's kingdom. Sita walks into a fire to prove she is pure, and the fire god, Agni, returns her unharmed.
In the last book, Uttara Kanda, Rama sends Sita away because people gossip about her. She raises their twin sons in Valmiki's forest home. Many readers find these parts very painful.

Readers answer in different ways. Some explain Rama's choices as a king's duty. Some say these parts were added later. Many retellings, including women's songs, tell the story from Sita's side and question Rama.

words.d: the seventh and last book of the Ramayana
the fire god in Hindu texts

look.title: Three Readers, One Passage
look.text: Reader 1: Rama had to put his kingdom's trust first. Reader 2: Many scholars think this book was added later. Reader 3: The women's songs I grew up with take Sita's side and ask why she was treated this way.
look.prompt: How can readers who love the same story still disagree about it?

check.q: Which book tells of Sita being sent away?
check.why: Uttara Kanda, the last book, tells this part.

check.q: Who returns Sita unharmed from the fire?
check.why: The poem says Agni returns Sita unharmed.

check.q: Which is one way readers respond to these parts?
choices: Some retellings tell the story from Sita's side
Everyone reads them the same way
No one has ever asked about them
check.why: Many retellings, including women's songs, take Sita's side.

lessons.title: Sita's Side of the Story
lessons.mainIdea: Many tellings, including women's songs and a Bengali Ramayana by a woman poet, put Sita at the center.
reading: For centuries, women in Indian villages have sung their own Ramayana songs. They sing them while working, at weddings and at festivals. Many of these songs focus on Sita's feelings.
In the 1500s, the poet Chandrabati wrote a Ramayana in Bengali. She was one of the first women known to retell the story. Her telling puts Sita's sorrow at the center.
Scholars say there are many Ramayanas, not just one. Each telling reflects its place, its people and its questions. This variety is part of why the story stays alive.

words.d: the point of view from which a story is told
a woman poet who wrote a Bengali Ramayana in the 1500s

look.title: Same Event, New Eyes
look.text: Tell the golden deer part twice. First as Rama sees it: a strange deer, a task for his wife. Then as Sita sees it: a lovely creature, a wish, and then fear and loneliness when she is taken.
look.prompt: How does the feeling of the story change when you switch perspective?

check.q: Who was Chandrabati?
choices: A woman poet who wrote a Bengali Ramayana
check.why: Chandrabati wrote a Bengali Ramayana in the 1500s.

check.q: What do many women's Ramayana songs focus on?
check.why: Many women's songs center on Sita.

check.q: What do scholars mean by "many Ramayanas"?
choices: There are many copies of one book
check.why: Scholars point to many tellings across places and times.

lessons.title: The Ramayana Across Asia
lessons.mainIdea: The Ramayana traveled to Southeast Asia, where it has its own tellings.
reading: Traders, teachers and travelers carried the Ramayana beyond India. In Thailand it became the *Ramakien*. In Cambodia it is the Reamker. In Indonesia, a Javanese poem tells it too.
These tellings keep the main story but change details. In the Ramakien, Hanuman has a bigger, more playful role. Dancers act out scenes in masks and golden costumes.
The great temple of Angkor Wat in Cambodia has stone carvings of the Ramayana battle. In Indonesia, many Muslims enjoy Ramayana puppet shows and dances as part of their culture.

words.d: the Thai telling of the Ramayana
the arts, beliefs and ways of life of a group of people

look.title: Ramayanas Around Asia
look.prompt: Which country calls its telling the Ramakien?

check.q: What is the Thai telling of the Ramayana called?
check.why: The Thai telling is the Ramakien.

check.q: Where are stone carvings of the Ramayana battle?
check.why: Angkor Wat has Ramayana carvings.

check.q: Who enjoys Ramayana performances in Indonesia?
check.why: In Indonesia the Ramayana is part of shared culture, enjoyed by many Muslims too.

lessons.title: Ramlila: The Story on Stage
lessons.mainIdea: In the Ramlila, towns act out the Ramayana, often over many nights before Dussehra.
reading: The *Ramlila* is a play of Rama's life. Towns across North India perform it each autumn, often over about ten nights. Many performances follow Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas.
It usually ends at Dussehra, the festival of Rama's victory. In many places, huge figures of Ravana are burned. Crowds cheer as good wins over evil. Fireworks light up the sky.
In 2005, UNESCO honored the Ramlila as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity. Some Hindu communities in Illinois hold their own Ramlila plays.

words.d: a play of Rama's life, often performed over many nights
the festival that celebrates Rama's victory over Ravana

look.title: The Victory the Play Celebrates
look.text: At the end of the long battle, Rama defeats Ravana. The gods rejoice, and Rama's allies celebrate.
look.cite: Retold from Valmiki's Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (Book 6)
look.prompt: Why might a play end on this moment?

check.q: What is the Ramlila?
check.why: The Ramlila acts out the Ramayana.

check.q: Which festival does the Ramlila often end with?
check.why: The Ramlila often ends at Dussehra.

check.q: When did UNESCO honor the Ramlila?
check.why: UNESCO honored the Ramlila in 2005.
